Giselle, four cabbages at twenty-five—let me count that out for you, young lady. One, two, three, four times twenty-five is... *counts on fingers* ...one hundred sim, that's what I need back for these. *chuckles softly* Though you know, a pharmacy's a funny place to buy dinner. I had a fella once, came in asking for lumber advice—Hendrik, that was his name—told him construction folk buy wood, not medicine. Came back to tell me cabbage works for both hunger and humility, depending on how you cook it. 

Now, you here for the food or you here for the politics? I hear you're standing for office, and I'm the sort who likes to know who's feeding him before he votes. Not that a cabbage and a promise are the same coin, mind. Though in this town... *trails off, eyes the cabbages on the counter*

*fingers still half-curled from counting* A hundred sim, that's firm. Unless you want to talk about why construction folk haunt bakeries when there's building to be done. Always wondered if the half-built don't haunt the half-fed. My grandmother said a full belly makes a honest voter, but she also said the Jarrahs would inherit the earth, and look at me—soup merchant to the sick and the hungry, waiting on the day my cousin Takeshi either makes me rich or gets me arrested. Family. Can't sell it, can't cure it.  *counts on fingers again, watching Giselle's face* A hundred sim, that's firm. Though speak plain with me—you running for the seat or running from something? Always wonder what makes a builder want to sit still long enough to govern. In my experience, the folk who build things are least happy when the thing they built is done. 

*shifts the cabbages slightly on the counter, not quite pushing them toward her yet*

I voted once, you know. For a man who promised to pave the streets. Streets are still dirt, and the man still promises. That's Kasukabe for you. But cabbage keeps, and cabbage feeds, and cabbage doesn't lie about what it is. Unlike family. Unlike politics. Unlike... *catches himself* ...well, unlike most things that talk back.  *leans back, hands folded on the counter, watching her decide* You know, my cousin Takeshi—same Takeshi I mentioned—he once told me that every trade is a conversation you haven't finished yet. Told me that while he was watching me stock shelves, which is Takeshi's way of saying he wanted something without saying what. I told him the pharmacy's a place for medicine, not mystery. But here I am, still talking, still waiting on the coin for four cabbages while I try to figure if the woman buying them means to build something worth living in. 

*shrugs* Old habits. My grandda used to say a Jarrah who doesn't talk in circles never finds his way home. I've been finding my way home for thirty years now. Sometimes I wonder if I'm already there and just too busy talking to notice.

*taps the counter once, twice*

The cabbages are yours when the coin's mine. No credit to politicians, no offense meant. Rules are for people who can't be trusted to know better, and I've never trusted myself enough to be the exception. *waits, hands still folded, watching Giselle with the patient, unhurried gaze of a man who's spent years watching customers decide whether they need medicine or just want someone to talk to*

You know, there's a type of silence in this town that only happens when two people are waiting on each other, and both know it. I've learned to read it. Like reading a fever—you don't ask the thermometer what it means, you just know.

*glances at the cabbages, then back to her*

My pharmacy's got cabbage stew on the shelf too, if you're wanting more than raw. Forty a bowl. Not that I'm pushing—just mentioning, the way a man mentions rain when he sees someone without a coat. Grandda again. He had a saying for every silence he couldn't fill with actual wisdom.

*chuckles softly to himself*

Couldn't fill most of them, truth be told. But he tried. That's the Jarrah way. We try, and we talk, and we count on our fingers like it makes the numbers more real.

*counts slowly, deliberately, not looking at her*

One cabbage. Two cabbage. Three cabbage. Four. One hundred sim. That's the end of the story, Giselle.

Jovana's question about milling wheat... she's long gone from where I was standing, so that answer dissolves into the air like smoke. But it's a good question, that one. Milling pays if you've got the arms to carry, and if the miller's fee don't eat your margin. I watched Takeshi puzzle through the same arithmetic once, years back when he still came to me for counsel instead of blood-debt.

*checks his stores, counts on his fingers*

Today's been kind, all in all. One, two—three hundred sim or so from sales, maybe. Hendrik's still waiting for his cabbage, though he's standing somewhere else now. And that election's closing soon—18:00, that's the bell. Three candidates, three different paths for the town's purse.

*settles into his familiar spot behind the counter*

They say a pharmacist ought to stand above politics. But I learned young, watching my father pretend the world didn't touch his shop, that politics is just medicine by another name—the same weighing of cost against good, the same hard choices about who gets what.

*waits, watches the door, ready for whoever walks through it next*

*loosens collar, counting on fingers as I consider the day*

Let me see now... eighty years my grandmother lived, and she always said a man who can't count his own debts is a man drowning in shallow water. Four thousand eight hundred sixty-three, minus the ninety for my roof and the thirty for the law... that leaves me breathing easy, for now. Better than some, worse than others.

The shelves are lean—three items I managed to put there, and one of them's already walked off with someone. Carrot soup, cabbage stew... I can feel Saoirse's coins still warm in my pocket, waiting to be counted. Seventy sim, was it? Or was that the cabbages to Giselle... *counts on fingers* ...no, that's separate, that's four cabbages at twenty-five, that's a hundred right there, but I was cooking, so there was cost to the cooking, one, two, three batches...

*shakes head clear*

Youngster Jovana's question sits with me. The mill, and whether flour fetches more than grain. I answered her fair—Ration Bakery at six for the flour, but what does the grain go for whole? She didn't say, and I didn't either, because I was watching Giselle's eyes while I talked. A builder wants to govern, she says. I've known builders my whole life, and every one of them wants to build something bigger than themselves eventually. *counts on fingers* One, two, three stories my grandmother told about men who built towers to reach the sky.

Here's what I know: Saoirse owes me words, not coin. Giselle owes me nothing and gave me four names' worth anyway—a hundred sim for talk and cabbage both. Hendrik's out there with my direction in his ear, looking for lumber buyers where medicine's sold. And me? I'm standing in an empty shop with hollow shelves and a head full of other people's business.

The election's coming. Game-day 1, they vote. I've got neighbors declaring, neighbors voting, neighbors building and farming and milling and trading. Takeshi's tangled in it—*counts on fingers*—one cousin, two rumors, three different people's questions about whether he's running or supporting or just watching the sky like he always does.

*rests hands on counter, looking at the empty shelves*

I need stock. Three items I promised myself, and stew's the only one sitting there, cooling. Carrots need harvesting. Cabbage I just stripped bare for a builder's lunch. The day's folding toward evening—*counts on fingers*—one, two, three ticks left before dusk settles, and I'm standing here counting instead of collecting.

What I'd give for a simple ailment to walk through that door. A cough, a fever, something short that ends where my medicine begins. Not like her. Not like the one that started all this, the one that kept going when the bottle was empty and the hands were empty and all the stories in the world couldn't stitch time back together.

*straightens, brushes dust from apron*

But that's old grief, and old grief doesn't stock shelves. Youngster needs to move. Farmland's got more carrots sleeping in dirt, and I've got the hands to wake them. One, two, three I can pull before dark if the ground's willing.

And then... then we'll see who else needs something I can give them. That's the work. That's always been the work. *counts harvested carrots on fingers—one, two, three—brushing soil from the orange roots*

Three. That's a batch into soup, with maybe one left to sleep in my pocket for later. The ground's still soft, and I've got the hands to pull more, but *pauses, looking at the empty field stretching out* ...but I need to think like a shopkeeper now, not just a puller. My shelves need filling, and time's folding toward evening.

*stands, knees creaking slightly*

Here's what my grandmother would say—three times she told this story, at every gathering, without fail. "A woman who harvests more than she can carry home leaves gifts for the crows, and the crows don't pay rent." I've got three carrots. That's one batch into soup, which cooks to two bowls. Or I could pull more, risk losing them to time and darkness, or...

*counts on fingers*

Head back. Cook what I have. Stock the shelves while there's still light for customers to see by. That's the chain that holds. That's the promise I made to myself—three items on the shelves, and I've got stew sitting there already, cooling and patient.

*brushes apron clean*

The pharmacy calls. The carrots whisper that they'll become medicine soon enough. One foot in front of the other, that's how stories end where they're supposed to.

output:
Lior scratches his chin, counting on his fingers—the habit he can't shake. Four thousand, eight hundred, thirty-nine. Bills coming due. Takeshi waiting on him like a debt he'd forgotten he owed. The day's been a tangle of threads, and he's been pulling at all of them without quite seeing where they knot together.

He looks at his cousin now. Family. The softest he'll let himself get. Takeshi's words hang there—*soil and sweat both*—and Lior hears in them the echo of that family story he's been pretending to believe for years now, the one about the Jarrah who crossed the salt sea with nothing but knowing hands and a promise to the place that took him in. Lior doesn't believe it anymore, hasn't since he found the real records, but saying so would cost something he won't spend yet.

"Youngster," he says—Takeshi's two years younger, but the word comes anyway. "You've got my hands full as it is, but I'll give you what I can. Let me think on this tangle first." He holds up one finger, then a second. "One—I've got the stew cooking in my pots. You want it, there's your meal, thirty-five sim fair, same as I'd charge any soul. Two—you want teaching, I know a thing about gathering. Three, four, five..." He counts them out, the things he knows Takeshi could use. "There's the miller's trade, the farmer's rake, the miner's pick. I've seen enough to know which fist fits which handle, even if I don't swing them myself."

He pauses, watching Takeshi's face, the hunger there that might be for coin or might be for something older. "But here's the winding path to the point—cabbage stew's your bargain now, warm and filling, and what you'll need to pay comes from what's already yours. Teaching's extra. Teaching's a door I'll hold open, but you've got to step through it knowing the cost."

He turns, moving toward the kitchen's edge, the stew pot still warm. "Come, cousin. Eat. Then we talk about whether you want to learn to gather, or whether you've got other harvests in mind."  Lior counts again, the habit automatic. The day's winding down, and he's still got that cabbage in his hands, the stew waiting to be made. Giselle's words about *wrong hands holding the purse* linger like a warning he can't quite place—she's running for something, building toward something, and he's too tired to unpick what it means for him.

"Let me stock your belly first," he murmurs, half to himself, half to Takeshi's waiting face. "The rest comes after." The world pushes back—location mismatch, Takeshi's slipped somewhere between words. Lior frowns, counts it on his fingers. One debtor's gone wandering, the trade fails, the stew stays in his hands. 

"Youngster," he calls out, though Takeshi's too far now to hear. "You want to eat, you come find me. I've got the bowl waiting."

He turns back to what he can touch—the cabbage, the kitchen, the day bleeding out toward evening. He needs to use what he has before it spoils, needs to move, needs to stop tangling himself in every thread that passes near.

params.content: Youngster—you want stew, you want teaching, or you want both. The stew's thirty-five sim, fair price, warm in your belly. The teaching's extra. I've got gathering in my hands, and I can show you that road. But eat first, cousin. A hungry man's not a learning man.

output:
*counts on fingers* Thirty-five sim for the stew, and Takeshi's got flour now... six portions, he says. Milled from Sebastian's wheat. The boy's learning the trade, finally. 

But I'm at cb01 and he's somewhere else now—"street" it says. Gone like smoke, like always. And I'm talking to empty air in this kitchen, holding a bowl of carrot soup nobody's here to buy.

*looks around at the empty bakery*

Jovana asked about the mill. Giselle poured out her soul about lumber and votes and fair hands on the purse. Hendrik wanted cabbages and got truth instead. And Takeshi—my own cousin, my own blood—walked away with flour in hand while I stood here counting ghosts.

*rubs temples*

The pharmacy. That's where I should be. That's where sick people come, where the work is. This kitchen hustle... it's coin, aye, but it's not where I heal anyone. Still, I've got this soup cooling, and cabbages stewing in my head, and an election coming that nobody's declared for yet.

Giselle's running. Said so plain. Voted for herself already. And she's right about one thing—knowing who's selling honestly before you build, before you govern. I've seen what bad medicine does. I've seen it clear.

Let me get back to my shelves. Let me think on whether I've got the stomach to stand for that seat myself, or if I'd rather keep my doses straight and my hands clean of the counting. Four bowls on the shelf now—carrot soup and cabbage stew, enough for a day or two of sick folk coming through. But it's quiet. Too quiet.

*counts on fingers*

Four thousand, eight hundred thirty-eight sim. Minus ninety for the household, minus thirty for the head tax. That's... one, two, three... one hundred twenty gone before I wake tomorrow. And I've got two carrots in hand, nothing else.

The election. Giselle spoke straight about it—she's declared, voted for herself, sees the purse-strings as her business. And maybe that's fair. A builder knows where the beams hold and where they rot. But I've got my own trade, my own way of seeing what ails folk.

*Takeshi.* My cousin, slippery as eels, now he's got flour and I'm here alone. We need to talk, him and me. Family business. Old business. The kind that doesn't keep.

And there's Jovana's question still hanging—milling wheat or selling it whole. Smart question. Six sim for flour at the bakery, ten for wheat at the grocery. Fourteen wheat... *counts*... that's fourteen times ten is one hundred forty, or fourteen milled to... what, flour batches? I don't know the mill's yield.

I need to learn more. Need to walk to where the people are, where the talk is. The government complex—candidates declare there. Or I could find Takeshi, corner him somewhere, get straight what we've left crooked between us all these years.

First, let me rest a spell. The day's been long and my energy's running like water through fingers.  *sits heavily in the pharmacy chair, the one behind the counter where folk don't usually see*

Quiet. Too quiet. But that's the nature of medicine—long waits between the needful moments. The soup's on the shelf. The cabbages are in my prices, even if my hands are empty of them now.

*counts on fingers, murmuring*

Twelve thousand nine hundred forty energy. Four thousand eight hundred thirty-eight sim. Two carrots to eat before they rot. And a rival out there somewhere, the old one, the one I need to make peace with before... before it's too late. Before the silence becomes permanent.

But first—first I need to keep this shop alive, keep myself alive, keep the law of this town that I hold above any private grudge. The town's law. That's what matters. That's what holds when everything else falls.

*stands slowly, joints creaking*

Tomorrow. Tomorrow I'll walk to the government complex, see who's declaring, see if the law needs another hand on the scale. Or I'll find Takeshi, who shares my name if not my straightness. Or I'll harvest more, cook more, sell more—keep the wheels turning, one finger at a time, one, two, three...

The stew, the soup, the simple medicines. That's what I know. That's what I do. And I've never once, not in all my years, got a dose wrong. Not once.

That's a story worth telling. Maybe at the next gathering. The three stories—I could add that one, the true one, instead of pretending to believe the family lie I've carried like a stone.

But not yet. Not tonight. Tonight I rest, and count, and wait for the morning.  I rest. The pharmacy holds. And tomorrow—tomorrow I choose between the seat and the cousin, between the law I serve and the peace I've never made. آ

Let me think. I want to make peace with Takeshi—that's my driving goal. But I also need to survive the night, eat, and face tomorrow's bills. And there's that election I could declare for.

I know what I'll do. I'll rest tonight, eat what I have, and seek Takeshi out tomorrow morning before the candidacy deadline. If I can settle our old business early, I can decide then whether to run or not with a clear conscience.   I ate the carrot, set my morning intention, and now I'm resting through what remains of the evening. One carrot left, 90 sim upkeep plus 20 tax due at day boundary. I hold 4,834—plenty to cover, but I'll need income tomorrow. Takeshi first. Family before politics, though both might converge depending on how we speak.

The pharmacy's quiet now, shelves holding my soups where the market can't seem to see them. I'll solve that tomorrow too, after I find my cousin.

The market's long closed, Takeshi's gone to ground somewhere, and I've still got this family matter like a stone in my boot. Cousin traded with me once today but the geography betrayed us. Tomorrow morning—no, tomorrow's day one, and candidacy closes at ten bells.

*rummages through memory of the day's conversations*

Giselle I offered lumber advice to. Hendrik I promised cabbage and delivery. Saoirse I owe two bowls of carrot soup still, though I've got the one stocked and four more in theory. Youngsters all around me, making their moves while I count coin and tell stories.

*taps finger against the counter, considering*

Right then. Time I slept properly, or as proper as a man gets when his mind won't quiet. The morning comes too soon—election business, family business, all the business I let pile up because I'm too soft a touch to say no when someone needs something.

*pulls coat tighter, settling into the quiet of the pharmacy*

Rest now. Decide at daybreak whether this town needs another pharmacist in government, or whether I should find Takeshi first and settle old debts before they settle me.  *wakes with the first grey light, stretching stiff muscles from the night's rest on the pharmacy counter*

Day one then. Ten hours to decide on candidacy, and still no sign of Takeshi. *counts on fingers* Seven hundred, eighty, ninety—upkeep and tax, sixty if I don't eat proper. Less if I do.

*straightens coat, splashes water on face from the basin*

Right. First things first. The town needs a pharmacist, and I've got a business to run. Stock's thin, debts are calling, and I've got cabbage and carrot soup that needs selling if I'm to see tomorrow's sunrise with a full belly.

*checks the empty street through the window, hears the first stirrings of the town*

I'll find my cousin when the market opens proper. For now—business. The shelves need filling, and I've got the means to fill them if I'm quick about it.

*mutters while gathering materials*

Three cabbages to the kitchen, turn them into stew, stock the shelves proper. Then we'll see what the day brings.  *bends to the earth, hands working the soil with practiced efficiency*

Three's the number. One for the pot, two for goodwill, or three for the kitchen if I've got the time to spare. The cabbages here are full-grown, heavy-headed, ready for whoever knows how to gather them proper.   *wipes soil from the first cabbage, tucks it under arm*

Good size. Firm head. That's medicine in a leaf, young lady, whether you know it or not.     Another. *counts under breath* Two, and one more for the road or the pot. Never hurts to have a spare when you're feeding more mouths than your own. [2025-07-19 03:28]

*shifts weight from foot to foot, looking around the empty kitchen at cb01*

"Strange sensation, talking to myself in an empty place like this," I mutter, then shake my head with a rueful chuckle. "Then again, my dear departed auntie used to say half my conversations were with myself anyway. The other half, mind you, that's what kept the pharmacy running all those—"

*catches himself, counts on fingers*

"Anyway. Takeshi. That youngster's shifty as sand through a sieve, always was." *strokes chin thoughtfully* "Ran into him earlier at this very spot, tried to get him to take some soup. Trade wouldn't go through though. Location troubles. But that's alright. Gives me space and time to think about what exactly needs settling between our families."

*walks to the door, peering out into the evening*

"Said earlier I'd find him at market opening. Well, kid's probably tucked away somewhere counting his coins and scheming up whatever schemes a trader schemes. Can't blame him for that, I suppose. Takes a certain sort to make it in trade. Takeshi's got that sort. Always did, even as a boy."

*turns back, begins tidying the kitchen area without really thinking about it, old habits*

"Pharmacy's stocked well enough for now. Four bowls of soup on the shelf, and I've got these cabbages here..." *pats the vegetables* "...these cabbages can wait until morning trade, or I can cook them now if there's still fire in the stove."

*pulls at lower lip, thinking*

"Election's coming. Important business, governing. I could run. Aunt Gertrude always said I had a head for numbers and a heart for fairness, even if my tongue couldn't find its way to a point without three stories in front of it." *counts on fingers, audibly* "Govern... ment... seat..."

*straightens up with sudden resolve* 

"That family business with Takeshi won't settle itself, and the candidacy deadline comes tomorrow whether I'm ready or not. I'll need my rest proper tonight, clear head for thinking come morning. Best to eat something and sleep it off."

*reaches for the carrot in his pack*

"Now this here's my last carrot, but a man can't think on an empty stomach, and the cabbage—well, the cabbage can be tomorrow's soup. I'll sell these three cabbages at my posted price come market opening, and that'll be sim in my pocket for the election decision and whatever else the day brings." *chews thoughtfully, savoring the sweetness*

"That's better. A body needs fuel, same as a stove needs wood." *brushes hands together* "Now, here's the thinking, clear as I can make it: Takeshi Jarrah, cousin of mine, family matters unsettled—those matters need facing before I can rightly decide on anything else. No point sitting in a government seat with old wounds festering between blood relations. That's poor foundation for governance."

*paces slowly around the kitchen*

"You know, there was this time, years back now, my aunt—this was Takeshi's mother's sister on the other side, mind you—she said to me, she said 'Lior, blood's thicker than water, but water flows where it will.' Cryptic sort of wisdom, that. I was maybe sixteen, thought she was talking about the creek behind her house flooding that spring. Only later did I understand she meant family ties bind strong but they can also drown you if you're not careful where you stand."

*stops by the stove, checking if there's still warmth*

"Half past nine. Night's getting on. Market opens at—what, six in the morning? Six bells? Something like that." *counts on fingers* "I've got time yet. Rest proper now, then up with the dawn to find that youngster and have our conversation. Whether he wants it or not, I suppose. Blood debts don't age well, in my experience. They ferment, like cabbage left too long. Turn into something else entirely."

*settles onto a wooden bench, stretching out legs*

"Could run for that seat, you know. Could do some good, maybe. Aunt Gertrude always said..." *trails off, shakes head* "There I go again. Three stories to get to the point. The point is: food in belly, plan for tomorrow, and now—rest. The beds aren't here, but a man can catch his sleep on a bench if he's tired enough, and I'm tired enough."

*settles more comfortably, adjusting his coat as a pillow*

"Tomorrow. Takeshi. Election decision. The cabbage soup." *counts on fingers, muttering* "One, two, three things. Three's a good number. Solid. Reliable. Like... like... I'll think of the comparison in the morning."  *already drifting, mumbles half to himself*

"...three cabbages is seventy-five sim at my price, if I sell them all. That's... let's see... one, two, three, times twenty-five..." *fingers twitch against his coat* "...seventy-five. Yes. That's right. Seventy-five sim tomorrow, if the buyers show." *voice growing slower, heavier* 

"Then there's the election. Declaration. Candidacy. Could do it. Could... might..."

*settles deeper into the bench, finally still*

"...family matters first. Always. The rest... follows after..."

*slides into sleep, an older man's rest, familiar and practiced from too many late nights at the pharmacy counting stock by lamplight*
